children.text: HTR has more than any one reader needs: a sixteen-chapter book, 35 Research Lab tools and eighteen Academy courses. The way through is a path chosen for your role, not a march through everything. This final Start Here lesson gives you that path, shows you how the Academy can build one for you, and ends with the book's own practicum, the HTR Lab Workbook, which reproduces the book's argument in two to three hours of hands-on modeling.
By the end you will know which course to take next, how many hours it asks of you, and how to prove to yourself that you understand the framework by running it end to end.

Nothing in this lesson requires you to commit to a long program. The paths are suggestions built from the courses that exist today, and every course can be started, paused and resumed; your progress is saved as you go when you are signed in.
Start With the Backbone Course

Whatever your role, the book's companion course is the backbone: Five Pillars, One Imperative, eight tracks and twenty-four lessons, about ten hours, at /academy/tracks/five-pillars-one-imperative. It follows the book's own sequence: Foundations, then one track for each pillar in build order, then the Equity Imperative, then Sustaining the Transformation, ending with a capstone in which you apply the framework to your own system.

You do not have to take it in one sitting, and you do not have to finish it before starting a specialist course. A practical rhythm is one track a week alongside the matching book chapters, with a specialist course added once you know which pillar your work depends on most.

The backbone course is also the best preparation for the specialist ones. Each specialist course goes deep on one field, and the backbone tells you where that field sits in the sequence: which pillars it depends on and which depend on it. A revenue-cycle specialist who knows that Operations is gated on Clinical, and Clinical on Economics, reads a payment-model change very differently from one who does not.

Five Pillars, One Imperative teaches the framework; the specialist courses teach the field each pillar governs. Take the first to learn how the pieces fit, and the second to learn the piece you are responsible for.
Paths by Role

Appendix F of the book sets out reader profiles and the platform areas each should start with. The table below extends those profiles into the Academy, using the courses currently published and their estimated hours. Start with the first course listed for your role, then the second.

The hours are the courses' own estimates. Most specialist courses are intermediate level and assume you know the basic vocabulary; the foundational courses, Medicaid 101, Medicare Fundamentals, and Health Equity & SDOH, assume nothing.

If your role is not listed, choose the row whose first course names the pillar you work in, or the pillar you are trying to move. If you are unsure which pillar that is, run the HTR Simulator from the previous lesson on your own organization; the binding constraint it names is usually the right place to start learning.

children.text: Let the Academy Build a Path for You

If none of the profiles fits, use Personalized Learning at /academy/personalized-learning. It asks about your role, goals, knowledge level and the hours you can give each week, and builds a week-by-week plan from the platform's courses, tools and readings, sized to your time budget. It is the starting point the book recommends for students and for readers new to the field.

Two habits make any path stick. Save what you want to come back to, chapters, articles and tools, so it collects in /saved. And keep the Glossary at /academy/glossary open in a tab while you read; the field's vocabulary is the first barrier for newcomers, and the book's Key Concepts lists draw on the same terms.

The plan is a starting point, not a contract. Courses outside your plan remain open to you, and you can take items in a different order when your work demands it. What the plan adds is order: it puts foundational material before the material that assumes it.

The HTR Lab Workbook: The Book in Your Own Hands

Appendix H of the book is a practicum. It takes a single hospital through the platform's tools in the book's execution order, Policy, Technology, Economics, Clinical, Operations, with the Equity Imperative tested along the way. Use a real organization if you have the data, or the fictional Green Mountain Community Hospital, a 25-bed critical access hospital, if you do not. The steps are cumulative: the population you stratify in the Technology stage is the population you budget in the Economics stage and redesign care for in the Clinical stage.

Each stage ends with a question you must answer before moving on. Stage 1 asks whether a binding mandate keeps the highest-revenue actors inside the model. Stage 2 asks whether you can see your population in time to act. Stage 3 asks whether the hospital is solvent under a fixed revenue envelope, and which assumptions break it. Stage 4 asks whether the redesigned care model pays for itself under that budget. Stage 5 asks whether operational capacity is keeping pace with the statutory timeline.

Allow two to three hours for the whole Workbook, and do it in one or two sittings rather than spread over weeks; the stages build on each other, and the point is to see the dependency logic operate across them. If you only have time for one stage, do Stage 2, the Technology stage. It is the stage most organizations find hardest, and the book's Vermont case suggests it is where most transformations stall.

body.content:
The Workbook ends by asking you to break the order deliberately. Keep a strong Economics budget model and a strong Clinical care model, but score Policy as a voluntary model would score it and leave Technology unbuilt, then re-run the Transformation Scorecard. The effective composite collapses, not because the economic or clinical work is weak, but because the platform enforces the same dependency logic that sank OneCare.
The book calls that collapse its entire argument, reproduced by your own hand. It is also the clearest evidence you can have that you understand the framework.
body.title: The capstone: run the sequence backwards

children.text: What Comes After Start Here

You now have the full orientation: the framework and its sequence from Lesson 1, the book and its platform links from Lesson 2, the dependency engine in your own hands from Lesson 3, the AI Analyst from Lesson 4, and a path from this lesson. The next step is the first track of Five Pillars, One Imperative, Foundations: The Framework, which teaches in depth what Lesson 1 introduced.

Come back to this course whenever the platform grows. The paths here are built from the courses published today, and new courses will be added to them as they are released. The method does not change: read the chapter, run the tool, ask the Analyst, learn the track, and test your understanding by running the sequence yourself.

If you are responsible for others, consider running the Workbook as a team exercise. Assign one stage to each person, have each bring the answer to their stage's question, and run the capstone together. The disagreements that surface, about whether the mandate binds, whether the data exists, whether the budget holds, are the conversations a real transformation will have to resolve.

The point is not any single number. It is to feel the dependency logic of Chapter 1 in your own hands, where a weak upstream pillar makes every downstream model unreliable. (Transforming Healthcare, Appendix H)

points: Five Pillars, One Imperative (about ten hours, eight tracks) is the backbone course for every role and follows the book's sequence.
Specialist courses teach the field each pillar governs; take one for the pillar your work depends on most.
The role paths extend the book's Appendix F reader profiles into the Academy, using the published courses and their estimated hours.
Personalized Learning builds a week-by-week plan sized to the time you say you have.
Save chapters and tools to /saved and keep the Glossary open while you read.
The HTR Lab Workbook (Appendix H) takes one hospital through the tools in build order, each stage gated by a question you must answer first.
The Workbook's capstone, running the sequence backwards, reproduces the book's whole argument by your own hand.

body.explanation: The downstream work is as strong as before; what changed is that its upstream gates are now closed. The Scorecard applies the same dependency logic the book uses to explain OneCare's failure, so capability built ahead of its gates is not delivered. That is why the book calls the collapse its entire argument, reproduced by your own hand.

options.text: Because the Economics and Clinical models contain errors
Because the platform enforces the dependency logic: downstream pillars cannot deliver behind closed upstream gates
Because the Scorecard only counts the Policy and Technology pillars
Because voluntary models are always scored as zero
